_about: Practical next steps shown under a reviewed guide's answer, split by side. Hand-written and short; every form named here appears in the official LTB guidance in corpus/ (checked Oct 2026). Status: needs review by a person (see /review checklist). 'letter' names a written-request template in realtor/web/static/letters.js.

tenant: Tell the landlord in writing what's broken, where, and since when. Add photos and keep a copy.
Keep paying the full rent while you wait.
If it isn't fixed in a reasonable time, you can apply to the LTB about maintenance (Form T6).
landlord: Arrange the repair. To enter for it, give 24 hours' written notice unless the tenant agrees or it's an emergency.
If the tenant or their guest caused the damage, ask them to cover it; if they won't, you can apply to the LTB (Form L2).

tenant: Report the pests to the landlord in writing, with dates and photos.
Follow the preparation instructions for treatment so it can work.
If the landlord doesn't deal with it, you can apply to the LTB about maintenance (Form T6).
landlord: Arrange treatment and give 24 hours' written notice to enter for it.
Give tenants the preparation instructions in writing.

tenant: Tell the landlord right away, in writing as well as by phone.
If the landlord cut off or withheld the service, you can apply to the LTB (Form T2).
Many cities also enforce heat and property standards by-laws; your city's by-law office can inspect.
landlord: Restore the service as soon as possible and tell tenants in writing when it will be back.
If you need to enter to fix it, give written notice unless it's an emergency.

tenant: Report a broken lock or door to the landlord in writing, and say how it affects the unit's security.
Don't change or replace the lock yourself without the landlord's consent.
If the landlord has locked you out, you can apply to the LTB (Form T2) to be let back in.
landlord: Repair a broken lock or door promptly; it affects the unit's security.
If you change the locks, give the tenant the new keys.

tenant: Keep a record of each entry: date, time, who came in, and whether you got written notice.
Ask the landlord in writing to give proper notice in future.
If it keeps happening, you can apply to the LTB about your rights (Form T2).
landlord: Give written notice at least 24 hours before entering, with the reason and a time between 8 a.m. and 8 p.m.
Without notice, enter only in an emergency or with the tenant's consent at the time.

tenant: Check that the increase came on the LTB form with at least 90 days' notice, and at least 12 months after the last one.
If you paid an increase that wasn't allowed, you can apply to the LTB to get it back (Form T1).
landlord: Use the LTB notice form (Form N1) and give at least 90 days' written notice.
Check whether the yearly guideline applies to the unit before choosing the amount.

tenant: You don't have to move out just because you got the notice; only an LTB order can end the tenancy.
Check the notice is Form N12, with at least 60 days and an end date at the end of the term or a rental period.
If the landlord gave the notice in bad faith, you can apply to the LTB (Form T5).
landlord: Use Form N12, give at least 60 days' notice, and pay the compensation the Act requires.
If the tenant doesn't move out, you have to apply to the LTB; you can't remove them yourself.

tenant: Ask the landlord whether they'll agree to end the tenancy early, and put the agreement on Form N11.
If they won't, you can ask to assign the lease to someone else.
Otherwise give notice on Form N9: at least 60 days, ending no earlier than the end of the fixed term.
landlord: You can agree to end the tenancy early on Form N11.
If a tenant leaves early without agreement, you have to try to re-rent and keep your losses down.

tenant: You don't have to move out or sign a new lease when the term ends; you become a monthly tenant.
To move out, give notice on Form N9 at least 60 days before the end of the term.
landlord: The tenancy continues month to month on the same terms unless the tenant gives notice or you both agree to end it.

tenant: Pay what you can as soon as you can, and get a receipt for every payment.
If you get a Form N4 notice, paying the full amount owing before its termination date cancels it.
Talk to the landlord about a payment plan, and get any agreement in writing.
landlord: Give the tenant a Form N4 notice for the rent owing.
If it isn't paid, you can apply to the LTB (Form L1); you can't change the locks or remove the tenant yourself.
A written payment plan is often the quickest way to get paid.

tenant: A landlord can ask only for a last month's rent deposit and a refundable key deposit.
If you paid any other deposit, ask for it back in writing; you can also apply to the LTB (Form T1).
landlord: Collect only a last month's rent deposit (no more than one month's rent) and, if you want, a refundable key deposit.

tenant: Take dated photos or a video of the unit when you move out.
Normal wear and tear isn't damage you have to pay for.
landlord: Document the damage with dated photos and keep repair receipts.
The last month's rent deposit can't be kept for damage.
To claim from a former tenant, you can apply to the LTB within one year of them moving out (Form L10).

tenant: Keep a written record: dates, what was said or done, and any witnesses. Save messages.
Ask the landlord in writing to stop.
You can apply to the LTB about your rights (Form T2).
landlord: Keep a written record of what happened.
If a tenant's conduct substantially interferes with you or other tenants, you can give a Form N5 notice.

tenant: You don't have to move out just because you got the notice; only an LTB order can end the tenancy.
Check the notice is Form N13, with at least 120 days' notice.
If you want to move back in after the work, tell the landlord in writing before you leave.
landlord: Use Form N13, give at least 120 days' notice, and have the building permit the work needs.
Pay the compensation the Act requires and respect a tenant's written request to move back in.

tenant: Keep a log of the noise: dates, times and how it affects you.
Ask the landlord in writing to deal with it.
If the landlord doesn't act, you can apply to the LTB about your rights (Form T2).
landlord: Talk to the tenant causing the noise, then follow up in writing.
If it substantially interferes with others, you can give a Form N5 notice.

tenant: Ask the landlord in writing for consent, with the name of the person you want to sublet or assign to.
The landlord can't refuse consent unreasonably; if they do, you can apply to the LTB (Form T2).
landlord: Reply to the request in writing. You can refuse only for a reasonable reason about the proposed person.
You can charge only your reasonable out-of-pocket costs for giving consent.

tenant: If you left things behind, contact the landlord in writing right away to arrange to collect them.
landlord: Before disposing of anything, check which rule applies; for an abandoned unit you may need an LTB order (Form L2).

tenant: A lease term banning pets is void in most rentals, but condo rules can ban them.
You're responsible for damage, noise or allergies your pet causes.
landlord: You can't evict just because a lease says no pets.
If a pet causes damage, serious noise or allergic reactions, you can give a Form N5 notice.

tenant: You can't be required to give post-dated cheques or automatic payments, but you can choose to.
landlord: Offer other ways to pay; you can ask for, but not require, post-dated cheques or automatic payments.
